title: Reddit signals ominous upcoming "changes” for old.reddit.com
gist: Reddit signaled vague upcoming 'changes' to old.reddit.com — the 21-year-old legacy desktop layout many longtime users prefer — framed as necessary to fight abusive scraping and spamming, following its July move to require login for Old Reddit access, and alongside a broader tightening of third-party API access that pushes developers onto Reddit's Developer Platform.

insights.claim: In a blog post, Reddit said that in order to protect its platform, business, and users from abusive scraping and spamming, it plans changes over time to Old Reddit — the legacy desktop web experience built 21 years ago — including in the short term continuing to require login to access it and migrating critical bots and moderator workflows to its modern stack.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding (citing Reddit blog post)
insights.so_what: Reddit is explicitly signaling a phased wind-down of Old Reddit's legacy infrastructure without committing to a shutdown date, which longtime power users and third-party tool builders should treat as an early warning to migrate workflows before deeper functional changes land.
insights.quote: In order to protect our platform, business, and users from abusive scraping and spamming, over time we plan to make changes involving Old Reddit, the legacy desktop web experience for Reddit that was built 21 years ago.

insights.claim: In late July, Reddit started requiring users to be logged in to access Old Reddit, with a Reddit employee saying at the time that Old Reddit's logged-out experience was 'a significant source of abusive scraping and automated traffic on the platform.'
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: This is the first concrete step in Reddit's stated anti-scraping campaign, and establishes the causal justification (bot/scraper traffic) the company is using to justify further restrictions — relevant context for whether the justification is being used as cover for broader platform monetization/control changes.

insights.claim: Reddit spokesperson Rosa Kim told Ars Technica the company is 'exploring different options' without providing specifics on what the 'changes' entail, and said there is no hard timeline but that Reddit will work directly with mods, developers, and communities that depend on its systems; this follows a June comment from a Reddit employee that the company 'can't promise it will be around forever,' despite CEO Steve Huffman's earlier promises to keep supporting the site while people still use it.
insights.speaker: Rosa Kim (via Scharon Harding)
insights.so_what: The shift in tone from CEO Huffman's earlier commitment to keep Old Reddit alive 'while people still use it' toward an employee saying it 'can't promise it will be around forever' marks a specific, trackable erosion of Reddit's public commitment to preserving the legacy interface.
insights.quote: we can’t promise it will be around forever

themes.theme: Reddit's broader anti-scraping and API-access campaign

insights.claim: Reddit has previously fought unauthorized scraping by suing Perplexity and Anthropic among others, blocking the Internet Archive, and restricting crawler access for search engines it doesn't have a deal with; it also began charging for API access in 2023, which shuttered most third-party Reddit apps and was stated to be aimed at stopping generative AI companies from using Reddit to train large language models for free.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: This establishes Reddit's multi-year, multi-pronged legal and technical campaign against unlicensed AI data scraping, positioning Reddit as an aggressive defender of its user-generated content as a licensable data asset — relevant to Reddit's data-licensing revenue thesis and its litigation posture toward AI companies.

insights.claim: Reddit announced today it is further restricting new requests for API access and requiring third-party apps to move to Reddit's Developer Platform, stating it envisions 'a future where all good, trusted automation on Reddit runs within an ecosystem that allows us to offer support and enforce our policies consistently'; per The Verge, developers building third-party Reddit mobile apps will still need to request API access, with no set date for when all apps must be on the Developer Platform, and Kim said the shift will apply to 'all API apps except the ones we explicitly grant exceptions to.'
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Consolidating all third-party automation onto a controlled Developer Platform gives Reddit centralized enforcement and monetization leverage over the entire ecosystem of bots and apps built on its data — a structural shift toward tighter platform control that could reduce the diversity of independent Reddit tools and apps.

insights.claim: The article discloses that Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica's parent company Condé Nast, is the largest shareholder in Reddit.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: This is a material conflict-of-interest disclosure relevant to weighing the framing and tone of Ars Technica's Reddit coverage, given its parent company's controlling ownership stake in the subject company.
